It works better that way.

beats.narration: Question one. A teammate insists that two identical prompts must return identical text. The right response is B: not necessarily. The model samples each next token from a probability distribution, so wording can vary even when both answers are correct. A says the model is deterministic. That's exactly what sampling breaks. And C and D blame streaming or model size. Neither one changes sampling. Question two. What separates model choice from reasoning mode? C: model choice picks which family member runs. Extended thinking is a per-call setting. B is the classic trap: extended thinking is not a different model. It's the same model, deciding to think. A and D make the levers one thing. They're two.

elements.text: Q1 · identical prompts → identical text?

✓ B — sampling: wording varies,
   both can still be correct
✗ A "deterministic" — sampling breaks this
✗ C/D — streaming & size don't change sampling
Q2 · model choice vs reasoning mode

✓ C — model = which member,
   thinking = per-call setting
✗ B — thinking is NOT a different model
✗ A/D — two independent levers, not one

beats.narration: Question three. Your classification task already works zero-shot. What do three added examples do? B: they add token cost on every single call, for little or no gain. Remember the discipline: examples fix broken output shapes. They're not seasoning to sprinkle on working prompts. C is wrong because examples never change which model runs, and D is wrong because nothing in a prompt disables sampling. Question four. Thousands of inputs, offline, lowest cost. That's C: batch submission with polling. A synchronous loop hits rate limits and pays real-time prices. Streaming, answer B, only helps when someone is watching. And D, a bigger context window, is about fitting more in one request. Not about throughput.

elements.text: Q3 · add examples to a working prompt?

✓ B — cost on every call,
   little or no gain

✗ examples fix broken shapes —
   they're not seasoning
✗ C/D — don't change the model, don't disable sampling
Q4 · thousands offline, lowest cost
✓ C — batch + polling
✗ A — sync loop: rate limits + real-time prices
✗ B — streaming needs a watcher
✗ D — window ≠ throughput

beats.narration: Now the scenarios. Scenario one: the same classification task at temperature zero, versus high temperature. The answer is A. Low temperature concentrates probability on the most likely tokens, so repeated runs agree far more often. But notice the fine print: never guaranteed, even at temperature zero. High temperature spreads the distribution, so labels and wording drift. B claims temperature only affects length. It doesn't. It shapes which tokens get picked. And one more thing worth repeating: on the newest models, you leave sampling parameters out entirely. Non-default values return an error. Scenario two: zero-shot keeps returning the wrong structure. Switching to multi-shot, answer B, shows the model the exact structure to match, and that usually beats another paragraph of instructions. A is the retraining trap. Examples are not training. Nothing persists between calls. And D has it backwards: examples add tokens. They never make calls cheaper.

elements.text: S1 · temp 0 vs high temp

✓ A — low temp: consistent runs
   (but never guaranteed)
✗ B — temp shapes token choice, not length

newest models: leave sampling
params out — or get an error
S2 · wrong structure → multi-shot?

✓ B — examples show the exact
   shape to match
✗ A — not training; nothing persists
✗ D — examples ADD tokens, never cheaper

beats.narration: Scenario three: fifty thousand documents overnight, nobody waiting. Answer C, the batch pattern: submit, poll, accept the latency, keep the savings. A synchronous loop would hit rate limits and tie up your application all night. And streaming buys you nothing, because there's no one watching the words appear. Scenario four: a long agent session where the context window keeps filling. Answer B, and this one matters in production. The window is a fixed budget. An oversized input is rejected before generation. Hitting the ceiling mid-generation returns truncated output with a stop reason. The trap is A: the model never silently drops old turns to make room. Nothing is dropped for you. Trimming or summarizing history is your application's job. And that's exactly why sessions that passed in testing can fail once real inputs grow.

elements.text: S3 · 50,000 docs overnight
✓ C — batch: submit · poll · save
✗ A — sync loop: rate limits, ties up the app
✗ B — streaming: nobody's watching
S4 · context window keeps filling

✓ B — fixed budget: reject up front,
   or truncate + stop reason
✗ A — nothing is silently dropped for you
trim / summarize history = YOUR job
passed in testing ≠ safe in production
